new_statements.quote: Aquest argument, que ha estat aplicat a la Romània deçà la Mediterrània, quadra molt bé amb el que sabem de l’accent en amazic, on no hi ha síl·labes de tonicitat veritablement predominant [n. 3213: Val a dir que, en el conjunt de Tamazga actual, hi ha casos que ens obligarien a matisar aquesta afirmació (cf. VYCICHL 1984); en general, però, des del punt de vista fonològic, l’accent d’intensitat no permet establir distincions fonològiques i, des del punt de vista fonètic, fins i tot si en alguns contextos es pot observar una certa preeminència en la tonicitat d’alguna síl·laba, en cap cas té una intensitat comparable a la que té, posem per cas, en les llengües romàniques.]
new_statements.translation: This argument [that a strong intensity accent favoured keeping quality distinctions in stressed vowels elsewhere in the Romance area], which has been applied to the Romània on this side of the Mediterranean, squares very well with what we know of the accent in Amazigh, where there are no syllables of truly predominant stress [n. 3213: Admittedly, across present-day Tamazgha there are cases that would oblige us to qualify this statement (cf. Vycichl 1984); in general, however, from the phonological point of view the intensity accent does not serve to establish phonological distinctions and, from the phonetic point of view, even if in some contexts a certain pre-eminence in the stress of some syllable can be observed, in no case does it have an intensity comparable to the one it has, say, in the Romance languages.]
new_statements.citation: Múrcia Sànchez, Carles. 2010. La llengua amaziga a l'antiguitat a partir de les fonts gregues i llatines. Tesi doctoral, Universitat de Barcelona, Departament de Filologia Llatina (dir. Ignasi-Xavier Adiego). 2 vols. + annex cartogràfic, 1440 pp. hdl:10803/1724 (TDX) = hdl:2445/41654 (Dipòsit Digital UB); ISBN 9788469375792.

new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both volumes are held by the project (Murcia2010_llengua_amaziga_vol1/ +); title page read: 'La llengua amaziga a l'antiguitat a partir de les fonts gregues i llatines / Carles Múrcia Sànchez / Universitat de Barcelona, Departament de Filologia Llatina', with the TDX licence notice, so the work and the open TDX/UB deposit are real. Quote located exactly at A's locator: vol. 1 the text layer (p. 499, running head 'V. ZEUGITANA i BIZACENA', page-number line 30372 = 499) 'Aquest argument, que ha estat aplicat a la Romània deçà la Mediterrània, quadra molt bé amb el que sabem de l'accent en amazic, on no hi ha síl·labes de tonicitat veritablement predominant3213' and n. 3213 at lines 30343-3034…
new_statements.relation_note: Only the vol.1 p.499 substrate remark; the phonology chapter proper (IX §2) is silent on accent/stress/tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Author asserts that Amazigh (Berber) has no syllable with truly predominant stress and that intensity accent is not phonologically distinctive, and uses this (together with the 3-vowel paleo-Amazigh system) to explain vowel confusions in African Latin inscriptions; by implication the ancient substrate language (paleo-Amazigh = Numidian) is taken to have lacked a strong/contrastive word stress. No positional rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: n. 3213: 'hi ha casos [in present-day Tamazgha] que ens obligarien a matisar aquesta afirmació (cf. Vycichl 1984)' -- i.e. some modern Berber varieties do show accentual phenomena.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog files this thesis under Numidian [nxm] and it is the live Glottolog's most extensive description. Its object, 'paleoamazic', is the ancient Amazigh (Berber) language of all North Africa as reflected in Greek/Latin sources and Libyco-Berber epigraphy, i.e. the languoid Glottolog calls Numidian plus ancient onomastics from Egypt to Tingitana. The accent sentence quoted below, however, is phrased about 'amazic' (Amazigh/Berber in general, present tense, citing Vycichl 1984 on modern varieties) and is used as a substrate/adstrate argument for African Latin; it is an inference projected onto the ancient language, not an observation of Numidian prosody (which the consonantal script cannot record).

sources.citation: Galand, Lionel. 1988. Le berbère. In David Cohen (ed.), Les langues dans le monde ancien et moderne, 3e partie: Les langues chamito-sémitiques, 207-242. Paris: Éditions du CNRS. (§1.15-1.16 'Histoire du berbère, le libyque, le problème canarien', pp. 209-211.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Gives the Thugga consonant system from Punic equivalences, discusses back consonants, pharyngealised series and occlusive/spirant realisation, then: 'Le caractère essentiellement consonantique de l'écriture libyque nous prive de renseignements sur le vocalisme, dont on ne peut tenter la restitution que dans certains noms propres, connus par des transcriptions en d'autres langues.' Morphology/syntax/vocabulary notes follow. Nothing on accent, stress or tone. Cohen's introduction adds: 'L'étude du libyque n'a pas livré jusqu'ici des renseignements importants sur ce qui est tenu pour l'état anci…

sources.citation: Février, James-Germain. 1956. Que savons-nous du libyque? Revue africaine 100: 263-273.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Nous connaissons tout d'abord à peu près l'alphabet -- ou plutôt l'écriture consonantique -- qui a servi à noter cette langue.. Mais qui dit «transcription» ne dit pas «notation phonétique»'; letter values, doubled letters perhaps for consonant length, the sign H as mater lectionis for final -us/o/u, approximate vocalisation only via neo-Punic matres lectionis; then onomastics, morphology (feminine t-..-t, plural -n, w 'son'), lexicon. Nothing on accent/stress/tone.

sources.note: Nothing on stress; notes the Libyco-Berber script is an abjad without vowels; word comparisons add vowels by normalization from modern Berber.

sources.citation: Chaker, Salem. 2024. Diachronie berbère. Aix-en-Provence: Presses universitaires de Provence (OpenEdition Books, doi:10.4000/16r54); chapters 'L'écriture libyco-berbère' (pp. 189-196, doi:10.4000/16r3x) and 'Les Libyens, le libyco-berbère' (doi:10.4000/16r4m).
sources.note: Script chapter: 'Les Berbères possèdent une écriture alphabétique (consonantique) qui leur est propre' (§1); 'une écriture purement consonantique est structurellement inadaptée au berbère.. l'interprétation est rendue très aléatoire car, en berbère, les voyelles jouent un rôle absolument fondamental.. les cas d'homographie sont innombrables' (§19). The 'Les Libyens' chapter is onomastic/etymological. No mention of accent, stress or tone in either.

sources.citation: Kossmann, Maarten. 2020. Sibilants in Libyco-Berber. Journal of the American Oriental Society 140(4): 875-888. doi:10.7817/jameroriesoci.140.4.0875
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: First-hand phonological study restricted to the seven sibilant signs (argues they encode distinct articulations, possibly 3-4 sibilants with a length contrast); notes the orthographic convention of not writing initial (or medial) vowels and a possible final-vowel marker. No statement on accent, stress or tone (none is recoverable from the script).
